title: The Francolin and the Tortoises

full_text:
Beside a marshy lake in the Mesopotamian delta lived a proud francolin—a swift game-bird with mottled brown feathers—and a colony of ancient tortoises who dwelt among the reeds.

Whenever the francolin darted swiftly across the mud, he would mock the slow-moving tortoises: 'Look at you, miserable creatures! You crawl half a pace an hour, carrying an absurd stone shield upon your backs, while I run like the desert wind and fly across the rushes!'

An elderly tortoise looked out from her shell and replied gently: 'Speed is a gift, neighbor; but steady patience and a strong shelter preserve life when the hunter enters the marsh.'

The francolin laughed scornfully and continued his proud displays.

One afternoon, a company of royal fowlers entered the delta with trained hunting falcons, nets, and archery bows.

The tortoises immediately drew their heads, legs, and tails inside their hard, thick shells, resting peacefully upon the muddy bottom of the reeds, resembling smooth river stones. The arrows glanced off their shells harmlessly, and the falcons saw only rocks.

The francolin, by contrast, panicked! He darted back and forth across the mud, fluttered his noisy wings, and took flight into the air, screaming with fear.

The fowlers spotted him immediately, released a swift falcon, and trapped the bird in their nets.

As the captured francolin was carried away in a wicker cage, he looked down at the peaceful tortoises resting safely in the reeds, lamenting: 'Alas! I despised their slow patience, but their modest armor saved them, while my boastful wings became my snare.'
moral: Patience and steady endurance achieve lasting safety, while hasty pride rushes into danger.
